blocks.text: I felt a deep spirituality from the Zapatistas. The Mayan language, as they explained, doesn’t even have subject/object structure. blocks.text: Escuelita Zapatista — The Zapatista school to teach outsiders their way of life

For the 10th anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened up the Escuelita (little school). The goal of the escuelita was to expand their anarcho-communal, spiritual-humanist revolution worldwide. Outsiders came from all over the world, lived with host families there and learned autonomy by taking part in day to day life. Around 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to later ones.

blocks.raw: Community Is What Makes Psychedelics Pl/ork Best!

blocks.text: Part of it is integration: an insight needs somewhere to land. What happens when you come back from an amazing experience which gave you insight and clarity about your life, into the same old environment where nobody knows what you’ve been through and you’re faced with the same old cues? It can be super helpful to have gone through the experience in a community, where the people who held you through it can also notice what happens to you over the following months. The deeper you go, the more alienated you can feel. After my original ayahuasca ego deaths at age 25, I had trouble finding anyone in the physical world who seemed to have experienced anything similar. I couldn’t even find them at Buddhist monasteries despite all the preaching about enlightenment. That helped give me a God complex, a Savior complex, or both, which then attracted exactly the right people to show me my limits. 😂 In a community of people who’ve sat through the same nights, you aren’t the only one who’s been there, and someone can catch the God complex early. Do you trust the people you’re relying on for support? Support from people you trust is different from paid support, which is often paying people you don’t know to look after you for a night. Sometimes they’re great, but sometimes the person with the feather has only known you for 4 hours and already has a cosmology to explain everything you say. In a community, your sober sitter may be someone who’s known you for years, and you feel the difference between being watched and being held. This is especially important when doing iboga or other long and medically risky experiences. For those you need to be properly screened beforehand and monitored continuously. Your peers can also reality check any downloads you may have had. Psychedelics can give you insight and they can give you convincing nonsense, all in the same bright shining light. A few friends who know your history may notice the difference between new understanding and… mom. One of the benefits of community is rhythm , and many traditional medicinal practices occur within ceremonies that have a communal schedule. The shared schedule of ceremonies, rather than each person doing ceremonies when they want, can serve to limit compulsive use and provide for integration time. There are the practical benefits: logistics are easier when it comes to things like having childcare arranged by the group that parents are comfortable leaving their kid(s) with, not needing to drive away from the ceremony, having someone bring water to someone or just sit quietly with them while they come back to normal consciousness, etc. And if you scream in release, the neighbors and landlord don’t call 911. And then there will be people to play with! Raves often let strangers fast-track intimacy (getting to a level of intimacy that usually comes after building trust), but imagine doing ecstatic music & dance in a community that already knows each other (and each other’s inconvenient habits). 💃🕺

blocks.text: Most of the writing on communities hasn’t caught up with psychedelics. They’ve gone from taboo toward regulated use really fast ( licensed service centers for psilocybin started opening in Oregon in 2023, Colorado set up a system for regulating natural medicines and began licensing in 2025, and New Mexico enacted a Medical Psilocybin Act in 2025), and Australia has allowed authorized psychiatrists limited access for a list of conditions since 2023, for both psilocybin and MDMA.

blocks.text: First, correspond with the visitor. Did they read the materials? (Not everyone does.) Do they get the basic idea of why this community is here? Are they at least starting to do the relevant practices? It’s a lot cheaper to find out through a thoughtful exchange than after six months of misunderstanding, right? The short visit: If they come for a week or two and just participate in normal life, well, most people can be charming for two weeks. Not exactly a high bar. 😅 So that’s about all you’ll find out. The long visit: If you’re not around long enough to actually experience inconvenience and conflict with the person in question, then you’re not going to learn very much about them. Watch how they react when working and making decisions in the group. When tired, corrected, attracted, disappointed, bored, etc. (Hopefully not all at once!) Even a professional faker may be able to pull off an act for months. Taking on responsibilities: If someone will have a role in your group that has serious consequences, involving kids, shared resources, medicine, vehicles or private records, you want to know how they handle that specific thing. I wouldn’t hand someone the van keys just because they’re great with kids. You can find out by checking whether you’ve seen them do this thing before, and asking for references if appropriate. Give people access to these things in stages and ensure there’s always some way to appeal decisions about these roles to a separate authority if needed.

blocks.text: One of the biggest reasons I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff’s The Continuum Concept . It’s one outsider’s interpretation of the Ye’kuana, an Indigenous people of the Venezuelan rainforest she lived with, and she may have idealized what she saw, but it’s still a powerful picture: the babies are carried along in ordinary adult life, the kids are surrounded by people of several ages and learn by taking part, and it doesn’t fall on one exhausted parent to be a child’s whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.

blocks.text: There are several parts to this protection:
blocks.raw: There are several parts to this protection:

blocks.text: Give children real agency. When kids say no, it counts. No grownup has a right to their affection, physical contact, obedience outside of legitimate safety needs, or private access to them. Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another trusted adult, whether it’s about a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. (A surprise has an end date. But secrets meant to isolate a kid aren’t allowed.) Teach Honesty . Protecting children is the duty of adults, but it requires children to help also. “The Boy Who Cried Wolf” is a didactic children’s story which continues to be useful generation after generation. The Buddha even taught his son Rahula honesty as the most important first lesson. I agree. We must teach children truthfulness before there’s a crisis. “Make believe” must be labeled as such. When adults lie to children (like “Santa is real!” etc), that teaches them to misunderstand the difference between reality and make-believe. Make sure kids understand what they say will be taken seriously if they are known to be honest. Those who are known to lie a lot are especially targeted by abusers who know their accusations won’t be believed. Don’t let the teaching turn into interrogation or punishment when they’re not sure. A scared or confused kid may get mixed up telling what happened and still need protection. Hear the child even when the accused is someone people love. Communities fail here, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or everybody’s friend. Decide on the response process ahead of time, before anyone’s face is attached to it. Keep everyone at risk safe first, right away, then make sure the accusation is investigated competently and fairly. Nobody’s status buys silence. Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. State intervention can fail spectacularly, and enclosing kids completely in a community can fail too. Kids need more than one world. In 1984, Vermont authorities raided a religious community in Island Pond and took 112 kids into custody over suspected abuse. A judge turned down the state’s blanket request to hold them, because it couldn’t name any specific case, and the kids went home that same day. There was apparently some physical abuse going on there as a disciplinary practice, but that’s something which varies a lot in every society also.

I looked through the research corpus for a well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to others. I was looking to find the reported conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I couldn’t find one. blocks.text: Amish young people, from about age 16, go through an indefinite period of freedom from parental control called Rumspringa . During this time they might travel outside, although they normally choose to stay in the community and begin acting as adults, including courtship. At the end of this period, they decide as adults whether to join the church, and roughly 85 percent or more of them end up joining . Pop culture makes Rumspringa seem like a wilder, more universal teenage free-for-all than it is, but the main point is that they’re baptized as adults, which means belonging is a commitment they make.

blocks.text: Unlimited freedom isn’t realistic, but it doesn’t need to be artificially impossible for grown kids to leave. Kids in or outside of intentional communities all need to learn enough about how the money world outside operates that they aren’t helpless in it. Like how to get a job, pay rent, read contracts, handle banks, get IDs, avoid getting scammed, and how to ask for help when they’re unsure about any of that. And all that sounds amorphous if it’s not structured into plausible next steps outside the community (school, an apprenticeship, work, family, another community).

blocks.text: Moving Beyond Money
blocks.raw: Moving Beyond Money

blocks.text: Like my father, I’m aiming for communities with less and less money involved, since money is antagonistic to the spirit of community. If I have money, I can get whatever I want, regardless of whether anyone cares about my wellbeing. That’s the hegemonic philosophy of life we are trying to overturn. I think the path there has three stages.

blocks.text: First there will be no money exchanged between members for basic community functions like food, housing, care, tools, education, transport etc. Members might have outside jobs, and they bring an agreed share of that income in. This is probably a good place to start if someone wants to create a community now and have it be realistic.

blocks.text: Later all wages and other income earned by the members from work outside the community, or from business inside the community, will be paid into the common purse of the community. No member accumulates private wealth while a member of the community. Some version of this is how things have been done in the Bruderhof community for generations, and my father lived there for 17 years. It is also done, in a somewhat different way, at Twin Oaks , and a number of other income-sharing communities . So a common purse isn’t just a theory.

blocks.text: Eventually, the community would also stop using money outside. People would meet their needs directly, or through exchange (be it trade, gift, work, obligation, or whatever). I couldn’t find a well-documented modern community that has gone this far, and in fact, it may be impractical in some locations because of government requirements like taxes on land. So perhaps the practical end point here is a community that is nearly entirely moneyless, but has a small collective cash boundary on the outside.

blocks.text: None of this does away with scarcity or economic power. There are lots of areas where such power can be wielded: access to food storage, housing, tools, land, medicine, transportation, and the outside world’s currency, to name a few. Even in a moneyless community, someone can control what’s scarce. Who decides how these things are budgeted and distributed? What do members owe one another? What happens when someone wants to leave?

They found the land, wrote the first documents, taught the method, recruited the first members, or kept things going when everybody else lost interest. Like the U.S. Founding Fathers.

blocks.text: A few things help keep that in check. One is to judge the method by results people can actually see. Will they see the members safely flourishing without being trapped? Able to leave without stigma? Can conflicts get resolved? Are the kids doing well once they grow up? And if the community is meant to spread, do new projects actually start up and last? Those questions seem more important to me than how big or old the commune gets, or how many decisions are made by consensus.

blocks.text: While founderism is a problem in every community, it’s especially so in communities which form naturally over time as I’m describing may happen in my case. In such cases, there’s no formal community and no formal rules until people decide to come together to make them. If there’s one other person who comes to visit, it also doesn’t make sense, so there’s a critical mass point at which people decide “we were just living together like friends, but now we want to formalize the community.”

blocks.text: “Nothing suppressed, everything processed” can become a situation where someone in the group must tell all, even if they don’t want to. I have seen that risk in groups that use the ZEGG Forum practice. A group starts out inviting honesty and ends up treating privacy as resistance. But privacy also can be resistance to the communal spirit, so there has to be a living, always re-assessed balance between what you and the community owe each other, and what remains your own domain. In general, people can have their own private practices, of course. But some practices go too far against the communal spirit. If someone starts worshipping Satan, say, they get booted.

blocks.text: From One Community to a Movement
blocks.raw: From One Community to a Movement

blocks.text: The problem of how these communities stay connected does eventually need to be solved somehow, if the idea is for them to spread without building another state. It should be solved in a way that allows help between communities and the movement of people and knowledge, and also keeps the differences alive, so communities can keep learning from one another. At the federation level, that outward purpose gets concrete: spreading healing practices, training people, seeding new projects, and keeping any one comfortable enclave from thinking it’s the whole movement.

blocks.text: The Federation of Egalitarian Communities (FEC) says it’s rebuilding, and that’s a good warning. It takes work to run a federation. Delegates. Records. Compliance. Coordinating resources. Holding meetings. Succession. Whatever dispute function it actually takes on. These things all take up labor and material capacity before any local crisis has eaten into both. If the legal or economic environment requires money, the federation also needs to have a cash budget for dealing with it. But the work of federation doesn’t have to be done by a single entity. Two communities might want to be closely linked as friends, and that doesn’t stop both of them from also being part of a general federation. There can also be local clusters, or single-function institutions like the FEC’s PEACH health pool , which isn’t currently governed by the FEC delegates.

blocks.text: Whenever a community or a federation creates or applies a rule, it’s best practice to store the full case history (with private details protected) so it can be re-evaluated in future: what happened, the principles that actually conflicted, your first judgments, and your final decision and rationale. Any dissenting opinions should go in there as well, along with the consequences in the case. When the rule changes because of a new case, run the old case through again to see how it would turn out. That saves each generation from having to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.

blocks.text: Experiment Before You Split Off
blocks.raw: Experiment Before You Split Off

blocks.text: Experimenting with a different rule doesn’t have to mean everybody goes out and buys new land right away. Try it inside the parent group first, then as a semi-autonomous project, and then, if it needs more independence, as a seed group nearby that still shares some tools, childcare, business or friendships. Splitting off completely should be just one step along that gradient, and nobody should have to do it just to be allowed to experiment.

blocks.text: Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution
blocks.raw: Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution

blocks.text: Leaving Voluntarily
blocks.raw: Leaving Voluntarily

blocks.text: Good people leave for good reasons -- dying parent, love, work, health, exhaustion, change of mind, etc. You don’t want them to lose everything they’ve put in. That’s coercive -- they HAVE to stay if they can’t afford to go, and a community of prisoners isn’t ideal. Whether or not you use money, you’ll need to have a way of providing people with resources when they leave (cash, if you use it, but also tools, transportation, temporary housing, stored up goods, the right to keep using something, or whatever). Otherwise their “right” to leave is only on paper -- it only works when the community happens to have spare money. Write up the exit terms while leaving is still only theoretical -- like a pre-nup when you’re planning the wedding. Not romantic, but protective. Much easier than doing it once anybody’s furious.

blocks.text: When Somebody Has to Go
blocks.raw: When Somebody Has to Go

blocks.text: A safe community can’t promise to keep everyone. There may be times when someone has to go. If someone is a serious or generalized danger to others, or keeps violating essential boundaries, or for whatever reason just makes everyday life together impossible for everyone else, it can be the right call to eject them. If restorative work can help in a reasonable amount of time, all the better. But it’s not the community’s job to be a treatment program for someone who’s endangering everyone else.

blocks.text: This power to remove people is so easily abused, though. So work out the process before it’s about anyone in particular. What counts as cause for immediate protective action? What protections will there be for the person’s interests (housing, records, family contact, access to common resources, outside funds if any) during the separation? When is it time to bring in outside help?

blocks.text: When the Community Dissolves
blocks.raw: When the Community Dissolves

blocks.text: Dissolution is something founders rarely want to talk about while they’re picking a name for their community and looking forward to its first harvest. Who would? But that’s exactly when it needs to be talked about.
blocks.raw: Dissolution is something founders rarely want to talk about while they’re picking a name for their community and looking forward to its first harvest. Who would? But that’s exactly when it needs to be talked about.

blocks.text: If the community dissolves, what happens to the land and any outside debts? What about its buildings, equipment, common stores or funds? What happens to each member’s agreed rights? More immediately, who is responsible for ensuring that everyone has a place to live and food to eat? Who takes responsibility for making sure people get their medications and the other care they need? Who keeps childcare going, and makes sure the kids’ schooling carries on? Who takes responsibility for transportation, for the records, for family contact, for the animals, for making sure land obligations are met, and for any unresolved claims? That’s a lot of loose ends!

blocks.text: Then there’s the so-called “Black Tax,” a strange legacy of the old communal system: if you’ve got any money at all, you’re expected to share it with your parents, your siblings, your cousins, to pay school fees, medical bills, funerals, etc. I understand the instinct. That’s how the whole organism survived (it wasn’t charity).

blocks.text: Communities That Abide by Dmitry Orlov makes an uncomfortable argument: the communities that last a long time often rely on 1) communal property, 2) separation, 3) boundaries and 4) a binding ideology. From a distance, cohesion and capture can look a lot alike. Is longevity alone a meaningful measure, when a community may keep going without its members flourishing? That’s the question in “Measuring Success in Intentional Communities” , a paper by Rubin, Willis and Ludwig. Commitment and Community by Rosabeth Moss Kanter is a classic. It compares a bunch of nineteenth-century communes, and the practices that built commitment in them. Alienation and Charisma by Benjamin Zablocki is field research on communes, and on the role charisma plays in them. Jo Freeman’s “The Tyranny of Structurelessness” (1970) is the classic essay on hidden hierarchy. Can it be harder to challenge than explicit authority? She argues it can.

edits.before_html:
1. Give children real agency. When kids say no, it counts. No grownup has a right to their affection, physical contact, obedience outside of legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.

  2. Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another trusted adult, whether it’s about a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. (A surprise has an end date. But secrets meant to isolate a kid aren’t allowed.)

  3. Teach Honesty. Protecting children is the duty of adults, but it requires children to help also. “The Boy Who Cried Wolf” is a didactic children’s story which continues to be useful generation after generation. The Buddha even taught his son Rahula honesty as the most important first lesson. I agree. We must teach children truthfulness before there’s a crisis. “Make believe” must be labeled as such.
    When adults lie to children (like “Santa is real!” etc), that teaches them to misunderstand the difference between reality and make-believe. Make sure kids understand what they say will be taken seriously if they are known to be honest. Those who are known to lie a lot are especially targeted by abusers who know their accusations won’t be believed. Don’t let the teaching turn into interrogation or punishment when they’re not sure. A scared or confused kid may get mixed up telling what happened and still need protection.

  4. Hear the child even when the accused is someone people love. Communities fail here, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or everybody’s friend. Decide on the response process ahead of time, before anyone’s face is attached to it. Keep everyone at risk safe first, right away, then make sure the accusation is investigated competently and fairly. Nobody’s status buys silence.

  5. Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. State intervention can fail spectacularly, and enclosing kids completely in a community can fail too. Kids need more than one world. In 1984, Vermont authorities raided a religious community in Island Pond and took 112 kids into custody over suspected abuse. A judge turned down the state’s blanket request to hold them, because it couldn’t name any specific case, and the kids went home that same day. There was apparently some physical abuse going on their as a disciplinary practice, but that’s something which varies a lot in every society also.

edits.before_html: The East Wind commune was almost the opposite way. There were maybe eighty people when I was there, enough to have a variety of personalities, small enough to actually make friends. I was happy there. I especially liked showering in a communal shower with both sexes present. I wonder if that still goes on at East Wind? That’s the sort of thing that doesn’t make it into the history books, and which takes some balls (no pun intended), considering how the wider society counts this as potentially damaging to childrens’ psyches, despite it being the way we’ve lived for thousands of years prior.

edits.before_html: If this article is going to be honest, it has to talk about both the value and the risk. Physical and psychological negative effects of ayahuasca were common in the Global Ayahuasca Survey, although severe effects were far less common and context mattered.
